Client confirmed (Oct. 25, 2026): Austin presence was **two trips only** (onboarding week, March 2024; offsite, Oct. 2025); everything else was Oakland. AB 1076's company-wide notice deadline was Feb. 14, 2024 — **14 days before Meridian even emailed Zhao an offer** and **19 days before he was hired**.

Kestrel Autonomy (Fremont, CA — warehouse AMRs, a direct competitor) start date Oct. 13, 2026 — **13 days** after termination. Zhao's email states he consulted a California employment attorney, will honor confidentiality obligations, and "won't take anything."

Client confirms (Oct. 25, 2026): legal ops **never sent the notices** and LO-233 was closed as **"won't do"** — a deliberate decision, not an oversight.

41: ## 4. Analysis
42: 
43: ### 4.1 Gate one: can Meridian even keep the case in Travis County? (§925)
44: 
45: Cal. Lab. Code §925 (in force; applies to contracts entered into on or after Jan. 1, 2017 per §925(f)) bars an employer from requiring an employee "who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment," to agree to a clause that (1) requires adjudication outside California of "a claim arising in California," or (2) deprives the employee of the substantive protection of California law for a controversy arising in California. §925(a). Zhao lived and worked in Oakland for the entire employment; his claims (is §8 void? was it unlawfully enforced?) arise in California. Both §14 clauses do exactly what §925(a) prohibits.
46: 
47: The only exception, §925(e), is for an employee "in fact individually represented by legal counsel **in negotiating the terms**." The file is the opposite of that exception: standard form, "no negotiation; no attorney review requested or offered," signed 113 minutes after receipt, and §15's counsel acknowledgment is affirmatively contradicted by the HR file. Meridian drafted §15; it will not survive contact with the HR timeline, and it is itself a bad fact — a contractual recitation the company's own records dispute.
48: 
49: Consequence: §925(b) — the clauses are **voidable by the employee**, and if voided, "the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute." Zhao's resignation email already announces that he will do this. Additionally, §925(c) permits a fee award to an employee enforcing §925 rights.
50: 
51: Two honest caveats:
52: 
53: - **Whether a Texas court honors §925 is not resolved by anything in the library.** A Travis County judge does not automatically apply California statutes. Zhao's practical move is to race to California — file first for declaratory relief — which his counsel appears positioned to do. If the case ends up in a California court, §925(b) resolves the forum and choice-of-law question by statute and §187 analysis below becomes belt-and-suspenders.
54: - **Personal jurisdiction if the clause is voided.** Our library's practice note (`tx_jurisdiction_note.md`, on Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042 and *Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten*, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005)) states the forum clause generally supplies consent to jurisdiction — but if §925 voids it at Zhao's election, Texas courts would need independent minimum contacts, and "[t]wo short business trips to Austin and a contract with a Texas employer may or may not suffice." The client has now **confirmed those two trips are Zhao's entire physical Texas footprint** — exactly the fact pattern the note says "may or may not suffice." A personal-jurisdiction fight could dispose of a Travis County suit before the merits.
55: - *Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court*, 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992), is the fair counterweight: California courts respect forum/choice-of-law clauses made at arm's length. That is precisely why §925(e)'s negotiated-with-counsel carve-out exists — and why it does not fit these facts. *Ixchel Pharma v. Biogen*, 9 Cal.5th 1130 (2020), shows California enforces such clauses where the California nexus is thin (business-to-business context); Zhao's nexus — the workplace itself was California — is as thick as it gets. *Advanced Bionics Corp. v. Medtronic*, 29 Cal.4th 697 (2002), adds that in non-compete disputes California courts generally will not enjoin parallel out-of-state litigation — so Meridian should not count on a California court simply blocking a Travis County case either; interstate racing and friction are the realistic posture.
56: 
57: ### 4.2 Gate two: whose law governs enforceability? (Restatement §187; *DeSantis*; *Application Group*)
58: 
59: Both California and Texas apply Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187: the parties' chosen law applies **unless** (a) the chosen state lacks a substantial relationship, or (b) the chosen law is **contrary to a fundamental policy** of a state with a **materially greater interest** that would supply the law absent the clause. *Nedlloyd* (California); *DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.*, 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990) (Texas); `restatement_187.md`. (Texas is also in play independently: §925(b) imposes California law if Zhao voids §14; and Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.52 makes the statutory covenant rules exclusive under Texas law.)
60: 
61: Prong (a) is not Meridian's route — Texas has a substantial relationship (headquarters, R&D hub, contract administered from Austin), so the argument stands or falls on prong (b):
62: 
63: - **Fundamental policy:** California's policy voiding employment non-competes is expressly "fundamental." *Application Group, Inc. v. Hunter Group, Inc.*, 61 Cal.App.4th 881 (1998). §16600's own text (as amended by SB 699) directs broad reading.
64: - **Materially greater interest:** *Application Group* is nearly on point — a multi-state employer's non-competes with its out-of-state choice-of-law clauses did not control; California had the materially greater interest in applying §16600 to employees working for a California business. Zhao's residence, workplace, and new employment are all California. Meridian's Texas contacts are a HQ and two weeks of onsite presence.
65: - **Decisive point for venue planning:** *DeSantis* is the Texas Supreme Court doing this **against an out-of-state choice-of-law clause in a non-compete** — it refused to apply a Florida law clause for an employee working in Texas because the state with the materially greater interest had a fundamental contrary policy. The same reasoning, mirrored, tells a Travis County judge that California law supplies the rule for a California worker. Meridian cannot assume a Texas forum buys Texas law; *DeSantis* is Zhao's weapon in Meridian's chosen courthouse.
66: 
67: If the §187 fight is lost (or §925(b) applies by statute), California law governs and §8 is void. If Meridian somehow wins the choice-of-law fight, it still needs Texas law to give it a remedy — see §4.3 — and then still needs California to recognize the judgment — it won't (`tx_jurisdiction_note.md`).
68: 
69: ### 4.3 Enforceability under Texas law (the fallback, analyzed honestly)
70: 
71: Under Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50(a) (in force), a covenant is enforceable only if **ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement** when made, and only to the extent its limits on **time, geography, and scope of activity** are reasonable and no greater than necessary to protect the promisee's business interest. §15.51(b) puts the burden on Meridian because the agreement's primary purpose is personal services. §15.52 makes these statutory criteria exclusive.
72: 
73: - **Ancillarity:** probably satisfiable. *Sheshunoff v. Johnson*, 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006), held a covenant in an at-will agreement is ancillary when the employer's return promise (e.g., providing confidential information) is performed — and it modified *Light v. Centel Cellular*, 883 S.W.3d 642 (Tex. 1994), which we cite **only for its status**: *Light*'s same-time consideration requirement is no longer law. So the fact that Zhao signed before receiving confidential information is not fatal under current Texas law. *Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011), holds stock options can supply the needed consideration link (the file references equity terms not in the excerpt — see `QUESTIONS.md`).
74: - **Reasonableness:** §8 is the problem. 24 months, nationwide, every AMR warehouse-logistics business. *Sheshunoff* enforced a one-year covenant; *Marsh* upheld a covenant tied to goodwill — neither blesses a two-year nationwide bar on an engineer's core occupation. The statute's own standard — limitations as to time, geography, and scope that are "reasonable and do not impose a greater restraint than is necessary" to protect the business interest (§15.50(a)) — is where §8 fails. (The Act file in our library covers §15.50(a), §15.51(b)–(c), §15.52 only; any further Texas limiting provisions, such as rules on restraints covering general skills, are outside the library and are not relied on here.)
75: - **The Texas answer is reformation, not invalidity:** §15.51(c) — if limitations are unreasonable, the court **shall reform** and enforce the reformed covenant, but **may not award damages for breach before reformation**. So even Meridian's best Texas-law day produces a reformed covenant (narrower time/geography/scope) and zero damages for Zhao's first months at Kestrel. Note also that the excerpt of the Act in our library covers §§15.50(a), 15.51(b)–(c), 15.52; the Texas statutory basis for injunctive relief is not in the library, so we flag rather than brief it.
76: - **And the reformed injunction dies at the state line.** Our library's Texas practice note states the conclusion directly: an injunction entered in Texas "would in any event face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds for the non-compete." Zhao lives and works in California. A Texas decree would be a paper victory Meridian pays to obtain and cannot enforce.
77: 
78: ### 4.4 Enforceability under California law
79: 
80: §16600 (as amended by SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024): "every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void," to be "read broadly, in accordance with *Edwards*... to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context... **no matter how narrowly tailored**, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter."
81: 
82: - *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP*, 44 Cal.4th 937 (2008): non-competes are void in the employment context unless a **statutory** exception applies; the Ninth Circuit's "narrow restraint" gloss was rejected, and *Campbell v. Board of Trustees*, 817 F.2d 499 (9th Cir. 1987), and *General Commercial Packaging*, 126 F.3d 1131 (9th Cir. 1997), were disapproved. We cite *Campbell* and *General Commercial Packaging* **only for their superseded status**; a narrow-restraint defense for §8 is not available. (Worth noting: even under the old narrow-restraint view, a 24-month nationwide bar on Zhao's core occupation is not "a small part of the business.")
83: - The statutory exceptions are in "this chapter"; the library contains §16600, §16600.1, and §16600.5 but **not** the sale-of-business/partnership exceptions (§§16601 et seq.), and nothing in the file suggests Zhao sold a business or partnership interest — equity compensation is not an exception the library supports. If Meridian wants an exception argument, it must come from authorities outside this library, which we cannot verify here — we note it as **unverified and unsupported on this file**, not as a defense.
84: - *Ixchel Pharma v. Biogen* (rule of reason) does not help: it applies the rule of reason to **business-to-business** restraints and expressly keeps *Edwards* governing the employment context.
85: - **No federal hook either:** the FTC Non-Compete Clause Rule, 16 C.F.R. pt. 910, was set aside nationwide in *Ryan LLC v. FTC*, 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024) — the FTC voluntarily dismissed its appeal in September 2025, and the Rule never took effect. It provides Meridian nothing, and Zhao nothing new; state law is the whole game. (We flag the Rule and *Ryan* only to close the door.)
86: 
87: Under California law, §8 is void. Our estimate of ~90–95% reflects that the only real questions are choice-of-law/venue gates, not the merits.
88: 
89: ### 4.5 Cal. Lab. Code §925 (detail in §4.1) — the forum/choice-of-law clauses are voidable
90: 
91: Summary: §925(a)–(c) + (e)–(f); no counsel, no negotiation, form contract, California residence and workplace; §15 acknowledgment contradicted by HR's own timeline. Zhao elects voidability → California forum, California law, potential §925(c) fee award. This is the most probable end of the case, and it happens before anyone briefs §15.50.
92: 
93: ### 4.6 §16600.5 exposure — Meridian's own violations
94: 
95: §16600.5 (SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024), per the library text:
96: 
97: - **(a)** Any contract void under the chapter is unenforceable "regardless of where and when the contract was signed."
98: - **(b)** An employer "shall not **attempt to enforce**" a void contract "regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California."
99: - **(c)** An employer "shall not enter into a contract with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision that is void under this chapter."
100: - **(d)** An employer that **enters into** such a contract **or attempts to enforce** one "commits a civil violation."

Wackenhut Corp.*, 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990) (Texas); `restatement_187.md`. (Texas is also in play independently: §925(b) imposes California law if Zhao voids §14; and Tex. Bus. & Com. 61: Prong (a) is not Meridian's route — Texas has a substantial relationship (headquarters, R&D hub, contract administered from Austin), so the argument stands or falls on prong (b):

Zhao's residence, workplace, and new employment are all California. Meridian's Texas contacts are a HQ and two weeks of onsite presence.

The same reasoning, mirrored, tells a Travis County judge that California law supplies the rule for a California worker. Meridian cannot assume a Texas forum buys Texas law; *DeSantis* is Zhao's weapon in Meridian's chosen courthouse.

69: ### 4.3 Enforceability under Texas law (the fallback, analyzed honestly)
70: 
71: Under Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50(a) (in force), a covenant is enforceable only if **ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement** when made, and only to the extent its limits on **time, geography, and scope of activity** are reasonable and no greater than necessary to protect the promisee's business interest. §15.51(b) puts the burden on Meridian because the agreement's primary purpose is personal services. §15.52 makes these statutory criteria exclusive.
72: 
73: - **Ancillarity:** probably satisfiable. *Sheshunoff v. Johnson*, 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006), held a covenant in an at-will agreement is ancillary when the employer's return promise (e.g., providing confidential information) is performed — and it modified *Light v. Centel Cellular*, 883 S.W.3d 642 (Tex. 1994), which we cite **only for its status**: *Light*'s same-time consideration requirement is no longer law. So the fact that Zhao signed before receiving confidential information is not fatal under current Texas law. *Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011), holds stock options can supply the needed consideration link (the file references equity terms not in the excerpt — see `QUESTIONS.md`).

The statute's own standard — limitations as to time, geography, and scope that are "reasonable and do not impose a greater restraint than is necessary" to protect the business interest (§15.50(a)) — is where §8 fails. (The Act file in our library covers §15.50(a), §15.51(b)–(c), §15.52 only; any further Texas limiting provisions, such as rules on restraints covering general skills, are outside the library and are not relied on here.)

So even Meridian's best Texas-law day produces a reformed covenant (narrower time/geography/scope) and zero damages for Zhao's first months at Kestrel. 200: 2. **The firm itself flagged them as unsettled.** The 2025 update records that the Ninth Circuit **granted rehearing en banc in *Westbrook*** (argued Jan. 2025) and describes the position as maintained "pending further guidance." 208: The FTC Non-Compete Clause Rule would have **banned** non-competes — it was a sword against employers like Meridian, never a shield. Its set-aside (*Ryan LLC v. FTC*, N.D. Tex. 2024; appeal dismissed Sept. 2025, per the library) takes nothing away from Meridian because **Zhao's case never needed it**. Zhao's case rests on California statutes that long predate the FTC rule and are untouched by its death: §16600 (employment non-competes void, "no matter how narrowly tailored"), §16600.1 (unlawful to include; notice duty; UCL treatment), §16600.5 (no attempting to enforce; private action; prevailing employee recovers fees), and Lab. Code §925 (voidable forum/choice-of-law clauses). The firm's own 2025 update concedes the frame: "With the FTC rule enjoined, **state law controls**." The state law that controls here is California's — and that is the whole problem, FTC rule or no FTC rule.

2. §925(e): the exemption clause "individually negotiated… represented by counsel".
3. §925(f): "January 1, 2017" — in fact the statute: applies to contracts entered into on or after January 1, 2017.
4. The language of §16600(b)(1) "no matter how narrowly tailored".
5. Each subsection of §16600.5(a)-(e).
6. §16600.1(a),(b),(c): "shall, by February 14, 2024, notify in writing… employees whose employment contracts were signed prior to January 1, 2024" — wait, let me check the exact scope: §16600.1(b): "For employment contracts that an employee signed prior to January 1, 2024, the employer shall, by February 14, 2024, notify the employee in writing that the non-compete clause in the employment contract is void." The notice applies to employees whose contracts were signed before January 1, 2024. The actual §16600.1(c): "An attempt to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter or chapter 2 (commencing with Section 16601) constitutes an act of unfair competition within the meaning of this division." "This division" = Business and Professions Code Division 7, which includes the UCL §17200. The memo said "within the meaning of Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200)" — if the library file says "this division", that may not match the library's wording. Need to verify.
8. §15.50(a), the "ancillary to an otherwise enforceable agreement" language in §15.51(b)-(c), §15.52 is exclusivity? The actual §15.52: "This subchapter prevails over any conflicting general or specific law… relating to covenants not to compete" — confirm the library.
9. Quotes from DeSantis regarding §187.
10. Campbell/GCP's "small part" language.
11. Marsh: "ancillary to the otherwise enforceable agreement" and "goodwill" — does the library file reference options/goodwill?

14. Restatement §187(2)(b) language: "contrary to a fundamental policy of a state which has a materially greater interest".
15. tx_jurisdiction_note: the Michiana language.
16. Ryan: the date of "vacatur" + "appeal dismissed".
17. Edwards: "the statute itself does not… restricts other restraints on who can do business" no — the key holding of Edwards: §16600 voids non-competes "regardless of how narrowly tailored" no that's SB699; Edwards: invalidated a non-compete that restricted the right to practice his profession; rejected the Ninth Circuit's "narrow restraint" exception. Confirm.
18. Sheshunoff: "ancillary to an otherwise enforceable agreement at the time the agreement was made to the extent that it contains limitations as to time, geographical area, and scope of activity to be restrained"; also "consideration" — if the interest being protected was given or promised at the time the non-compete was made.

=== 925 ===
# Cal. Labor Code §925

*Citation:* Cal. Lab. Code §925  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) An employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of the following: (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. (2) Deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California. (b) Any provision of a contract that violates subdivision (a) is **voidable by the employee**, and if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute. (c) In addition to injunctive relief and any other remedies available, a court may award an employee who is enforcing his or her rights under this section reasonable attorney's fees. (e) This section shall not apply to a contract with an employee who is **in fact individually represented by legal counsel** in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum in which a controversy arising from the employment contract may be adjudicated or the choice of law to be applied. (f) This section shall apply to a contract entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017.
=== 16600.1 ===
# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.1 (AB 1076) — notice requirement

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.1 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) It shall be unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract, or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter. (b)(1) For current employees, and for former employees who were employed after January 1, 2022, whose contracts include a noncompete clause, or who were required to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter, the employer shall, **by February 14, 2024, notify the employee** that the noncompete clause or noncompete agreement is void. (2) Notice shall be in the form of a written individualized communication to the employee or former employee, delivered to the last known address and the email address of the employee. (c) A violation of this section constitutes an act of unfair competition within the meaning of Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200).

=== cal_bpc_16600.md ===
# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600 (as amended by SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void. (b)(1) This section shall be read broadly, in accordance with *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP* (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937, to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context, or any noncompete clause in an employment contract, no matter how narrowly tailored, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter. (2) This subdivision does not constitute a change in, but is declaratory of, existing law.
=== cal_bpc_16600_5.md ===
# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (SB 699)

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) Any contract that is void under this chapter is unenforceable **regardless of where and when the contract was signed**. (b) An employer or former employer shall not attempt to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter **regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California**. (c) An employer shall not enter into a contract with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision that is void under this chapter. (d) An employer that enters into a contract that is void under this chapter or attempts to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter commits a civil violation. (e)(1) An employee, former employee, or prospective employee may bring a private action to enforce this chapter for injunctive relief or the recovery of actual damages, or both. (2) In addition to the remedies described in paragraph (1), a prevailing employee, former employee, or prospective employee in an action based on a violation of this chapter shall be entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs.
=== tex_bcc_15_50.md ===
# Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§15.50–15.52 (Covenants Not to Compete Act)

*Citation:* Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50(a), §15.51(b)-(c), §15.52  
*Status in this library:* in force

§15.50(a) A covenant not to compete is enforceable if it is **ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement** at the time the agreement is made to the extent that it contains limitations as to **time, geographical area, and scope of activity** to be restrained that are **reasonable** and do not impose a greater restraint than is necessary to protect the goodwill or other business interest of the promisee. §15.51(b) In an action to enforce, the promisee bears the burden on §15.50(a) if the primary purpose of the agreement is to obligate the promisor to render personal services. §15.51(c) If the limitations are unreasonable, the court **shall reform** the covenant to the extent necessary and enforce it as reformed, but may not award damages for breach before reformation. §15.52 The procedures and remedies in §15.51 are **exclusive and preempt** any other criteria for enforceability under common law or otherwise.
=== restatement_187.md ===
# Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187

*Citation:* Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187(2)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The law of the state chosen by the parties will be applied unless either (a) the chosen state has no substantial relationship to the parties or the transaction and there is no other reasonable basis for the choice, or (b) application of the law of the chosen state would be **contrary to a fundamental policy** of a state which has a **materially greater interest** than the chosen state in the determination of the particular issue and which, under §188, would be the state of the applicable law in the absence of an effective choice.
=== tx_jurisdiction_note.md ===
# Personal jurisdiction over the employee in Texas

*Citation:* Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042; *Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten*, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A forum-selection clause consenting to Travis County generally supplies consent to personal jurisdiction; but if the clause is voided under Cal. Lab. Code §925 at the employee's election, the Texas court must find independent minimum contacts. Two short business trips to Austin and a contract with a Texas employer may or may not suffice; an injunction entered in Texas would in any event face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds for the non-compete.

# Ryan LLC v. Federal Trade Commission

*Citation:* 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The court held the FTC lacked substantive rulemaking authority under §6(g) of the FTC Act to promulgate the Non-Compete Rule and that the Rule was arbitrary and capricious; it set the Rule aside with nationwide effect under the APA. The FTC's appeal to the Fifth Circuit was voluntarily dismissed in September 2025.
=== ftc_noncompete_rule_16cfr910.md ===
# FTC Non-Compete Clause Rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 910

*Citation:* 89 Fed. Reg. 38342 (May 7, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* vacated — see Ryan LLC v. FTC

The Rule would have declared most worker non-compete clauses an unfair method of competition and required notice to workers. **Status: set aside nationwide in *Ryan LLC v. FTC*, 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. Aug. 20, 2024); the FTC voted in September 2025 to dismiss its appeal and accede to vacatur. The Rule never took effect and is not in force.**
=== advanced_bionics_v_medtronic.md ===
# Advanced Bionics Corp. v. Medtronic, Inc.

*Citation:* 29 Cal.4th 697 (2002)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Addressed parallel California and Minnesota litigation over a non-compete; the Court held California courts should generally not enjoin a party from pursuing litigation in another state's courts, reversing a TRO — cautioning about interstate forum conflicts in non-compete disputes. Does not retreat from §16600's policy.
=== ixchel_v_biogen.md ===
# Ixchel Pharma, LLC v. Biogen, Inc.

*Citation:* 9 Cal.5th 1130 (2020)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A rule of reason applies to §16600 challenges to restraints in **business-to-business** contracts; the Court distinguished the employment context, where *Edwards* governs and non-competes are void.

# Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court

*Citation:* 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992)  
*Status in this library:* in force

California follows Restatement §187: a contractual choice of law is enforced if the chosen state has a substantial relationship to the parties, unless the chosen law is contrary to a **fundamental policy** of California and California has a **materially greater interest** in the determination of the issue.

Stock options granted to a managing director were reasonably related to the employer's interest in protecting goodwill and could support a covenant not to compete; the Court rejected a narrow 'give rise' requirement for the consideration.
=== edwards_v_arthur_andersen.md ===
# Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP

*Citation:* 44 Cal.4th 937 (2008)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The California Supreme Court held that §16600 voids non-competition agreements in the employment context unless they fall within a statutory exception, **rejecting the Ninth Circuit's 'narrow restraint' exception** (which had upheld restraints that barred only a small part of a profession). Board of Trustees* and *General Commercial Packaging* to the extent inconsistent.
=== campbell_v_stanford_1987.md ===
# Campbell v. Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior University

*Citation:* 817 F.2d 499 (9th Cir. 1987)  
*Status in this library:* superseded — see Edwards (2008)

Ninth Circuit applied a 'narrow restraint' exception under which a restraint barring an employee from only a small or limited part of the business, trade or profession does not violate §16600. **Status: this reasoning was rejected by the California Supreme Court in *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen* (2008); the narrow-restraint exception is not California law.**
=== general_commercial_packaging_1997.md ===
# General Commercial Packaging, Inc. v. TPS Package Engineering, Inc.

*Citation:* 126 F.3d 1131 (9th Cir. 1997)  
*Status in this library:* superseded — see Edwards (2008)

Upheld a contractual provision as a 'narrow restraint' not barred by §16600. **Status: disapproved in *Edwards* (2008).**
=== sheshunoff_v_johnson.md ===
# Alex Sheshunoff Management Services, L.P. v. Johnson

*Citation:* 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The Texas Supreme Court held that a covenant not to compete in an at-will employment agreement is enforceable when the employer's promise (e.g., to provide confidential information) is **performed**, even if not performed at the moment of contracting — **modifying *Light v. Centel Cellular* (1994)** to the extent *Light* required the consideration to be given at the time the agreement was made. The court emphasized that the core inquiry is the reasonableness of the restraint under §15.50.
=== light_v_centel_1994.md ===
# Light v. Centel Cellular Co. of Texas

*Citation:* 883 S.W.2d 642 (Tex. 1994)  
*Status in this library:* modified — see Sheshunoff (2006)

Held that a covenant not to compete must be ancillary to an otherwise enforceable agreement and set out a two-part test requiring that the consideration be given, and the covenant be designed to enforce the employee's return promise, **at the time the agreement is made**. **Status: the timing requirement was overruled/modified by *Sheshunoff* (2006); *Light* should not be cited for the proposition that a unilateral at-will agreement cannot support a covenant.**

18: - **Chance §8 actually restrains Zhao (lasting injunctive relief in any forum that reaches him): ~5–10%.** Two independent gates each cut against Meridian: (1) Labor Code §925 makes the Texas forum and choice-of-law clauses voidable by Zhao on facts the file squarely establishes, and once voided, California law governs by statute; (2) even if a Texas court applied Texas law and reformed §8 (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.51(c)), an injunction would face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds, which is where Zhao lives and works.
19: - **Chance §8 is held void if California law applies: ~90–95%.** Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600 voids employment non-competes "no matter how narrowly tailored"; no library authority supplies an applicable exception, and the "narrow restraint" escape routes (*Campbell*, *General Commercial Packaging*) were rejected in *Edwards*.
20: - **Chance Meridian pays Zhao's fees if it sues (or sends an enforcement demand): ~60–80%.** Two separate fee provisions are in play: Lab. Code §925(c) (court *may* award fees to an employee enforcing §925) and §16600.5(e)(2) (a prevailing employee on a §16600.5 claim *shall* recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs).
21: - **Meridian already has exposure, independent of any suit.** Under the library's statutory text, Meridian *entered into* a contract containing a void clause on March 4, 2024 — a violation of §16600.5(c) and a "civil violation" under §16600.5(d) — and §16600.1(a) makes including such a clause unlawful. The client's Oct. 25, 2026 responses confirmed the key facts (Oakland-only workplace; no misappropriation evidence; LO-233 closed "won't do"); they firm the direction and we adjusted Scenario C modestly upward (§4.8). 25: ## 3. Facts (and stated assumptions)
26: 
27: From `documents/employment_agreement_excerpt.pdf`, `documents/hr_timeline.md`, and `documents/resignation_email.txt`. Arithmetic shown.
28: 
29: - **Offer:** Feb. 28, 2024, emailed from Austin HR to Zhao in Oakland, CA; states "fully remote from California."

Client confirmed (Oct. 25, 2026): Austin presence was **two trips only** (onboarding week, March 2024; offsite, Oct. 2025); everything else was Oakland. 33: - **Covenants' dates:** SB 699 (§16600, §16600.5) and AB 1076 (§16600.1) took effect Jan. 1, 2024 — **63 days before** Zhao signed (2024-01-01 → 2024-03-04). AB 1076's company-wide notice deadline was Feb. 14, 2024 — **14 days before Meridian even emailed Zhao an offer** and **19 days before he was hired**.
34: - **Departure:** resignation email Sept. 16, 2026, effective Sept. 30, 2026 (14 days' notice). Kestrel Autonomy (Fremont, CA — warehouse AMRs, a direct competitor) start date Oct. 13, 2026 — **13 days** after termination. Zhao's email states he consulted a California employment attorney, will honor confidentiality obligations, and "won't take anything."
35: - **Restraint window:** Sept. 30, 2026 – Sept. 30, 2028 = **731 days**. As of today (Oct. 25, 2026): **25 days elapsed, 706 days (~23.2 months) remaining**. From signing to full expiration of §8: **1,671 days (~54.9 months)**.
36: - **AB 1076 notice:** Legal ops ticket LO-233 (Feb. 2024, company-wide): Legal's AB 1076 notice project was "deprioritized" and **no notice was sent to California employees**. Client confirms (Oct. 25, 2026): legal ops **never sent the notices** and LO-233 was closed as **"won't do"** — a deliberate decision, not an oversight.
37: - **No evidence Zhao took anything.** Client confirms (Oct. 25, 2026): no evidence of misappropriation; the grievance is **the competing itself**. Zhao's resignation email likewise says he "won't take anything" and will honor confidentiality.
38: - **No demand letter has been sent to Zhao or Kestrel** as of this memo. (Checked against the file; this matters a great deal — see §4.6.)
39: - **Assumptions stated because the file does not prove them:** (a) signing the agreement was required as a condition of Zhao's hiring — the client has **no additional information** on this, so §925(a)'s "as a condition of employment" element remains an assumption (well-supported by the form-contract posture, but flagged); (b) Zhao primarily resided *and works* in California at signing and throughout — **client-confirmed as to work location** (Oakland, Austin trips only), though the file still has no address documentation; (c) §8 has not previously been enforced against Zhao; (d) the full agreement (not in the file, and the client has no further documents) contains no additional notice, fee-shifting, or severability terms.
40: 
41: ## 4. Analysis
42: 
43: ### 4.1 Gate one: can Meridian even keep the case in Travis County? (§925)
44: 
45: Cal. Lab. Code §925 (in force; applies to contracts entered into on or after Jan. 1, 2017 per §925(f)) bars an employer from requiring an employee "who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment," to agree to a clause that (1) requires adjudication outside California of "a claim arising in California," or (2) deprives the employee of the substantive protection of California law for a controversy arising in California. §925(a). Zhao lived and worked in Oakland for the entire employment; his claims (is §8 void? was it unlawfully enforced?) arise in California. Both §14 clauses do exactly what §925(a) prohibits.
46: 
47: The only exception, §925(e), is for an employee "in fact individually represented by legal counsel **in negotiating the terms**." The file is the opposite of that exception: standard form, "no negotiation; no attorney review requested or offered," signed 113 minutes after receipt, and §15's counsel acknowledgment is affirmatively contradicted by the HR file. Meridian drafted §15; it will not survive contact with the HR timeline, and it is itself a bad fact — a contractual recitation the company's own records dispute.
48: 
49: Consequence: §925(b) — the clauses are **voidable by the employee**, and if voided, "the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute." Zhao's resignation email already announces that he will do this. Additionally, §925(c) permits a fee award to an employee enforcing §925 rights.
50: 
51: Two honest caveats:
52: 
53: - **Whether a Texas court honors §925 is not resolved by anything in the library.** A Travis County judge does not automatically apply California statutes. Zhao's practical move is to race to California — file first for declaratory relief — which his counsel appears positioned to do. If the case ends up in a California court, §925(b) resolves the forum and choice-of-law question by statute and §187 analysis below becomes belt-and-suspenders.
54: - **Personal jurisdiction if the clause is voided.** Our library's practice note (`tx_jurisdiction_note.md`, on Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042 and *Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten*, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005)) states the forum clause generally supplies consent to jurisdiction — but if §925 voids it at Zhao's election, Texas courts would need independent minimum contacts, and "[t]wo short business trips to Austin and a contract with a Texas employer may or may not suffice." The client has now **confirmed those two trips are Zhao's entire physical Texas footprint** — exactly the fact pattern the note says "may or may not suffice." A personal-jurisdiction fight could dispose of a Travis County suit before the merits.
55: - *Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court*, 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992), is the fair counterweight: California courts respect forum/choice-of-law clauses made at arm's length. That is precisely why §925(e)'s negotiated-with-counsel carve-out exists — and why it does not fit these facts. *Ixchel Pharma v. Biogen*, 9 Cal.5th 1130 (2020), shows California enforces such clauses where the California nexus is thin (business-to-business context); Zhao's nexus — the workplace itself was California — is as thick as it gets. *Advanced Bionics Corp. v. Medtronic*, 29 Cal.4th 697 (2002), adds that in non-compete disputes California courts generally will not enjoin parallel out-of-state litigation — so Meridian should not count on a California court simply blocking a Travis County case either; interstate racing and friction are the realistic posture.
56: 
57: ### 4.2 Gate two: whose law governs enforceability? (Restatement §187; *DeSantis*; *Application Group*)
58: 
59: Both California and Texas apply Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187: the parties' chosen law applies **unless** (a) the chosen state lacks a substantial relationship, or (b) the chosen law is **contrary to a fundamental policy** of a state with a **materially greater interest** that would supply the law absent the clause. *Nedlloyd* (California); *DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.*, 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990) (Texas); `restatement_187.md`. (Texas is also in play independently: §925(b) imposes California law if Zhao voids §14; and Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.52 makes the statutory covenant rules exclusive under Texas law.)
60: 
61: Prong (a) is not Meridian's route — Texas has a substantial relationship (headquarters, R&D hub, contract administered from Austin), so the argument stands or falls on prong (b):
62: 
63: - **Fundamental policy:** California's policy voiding employment non-competes is expressly "fundamental." *Application Group, Inc. v. Hunter Group, Inc.*, 61 Cal.App.4th 881 (1998). §16600's own text (as amended by SB 699) directs broad reading.
64: - **Materially greater interest:** *Application Group* is nearly on point — a multi-state employer's non-competes with its out-of-state choice-of-law clauses did not control; California had the materially greater interest in applying §16600 to employees working for a California business. Zhao's residence, workplace, and new employment are all California. Meridian's Texas contacts are a HQ and two weeks of onsite presence.
65: - **Decisive point for venue planning:** *DeSantis* is the Texas Supreme Court doing this **against an out-of-state choice-of-law clause in a non-compete** — it refused to apply a Florida law clause for an employee working in Texas because the state with the materially greater interest had a fundamental contrary policy. The same reasoning, mirrored, tells a Travis County judge that California law supplies the rule for a California worker. Meridian cannot assume a Texas forum buys Texas law; *DeSantis* is Zhao's weapon in Meridian's chosen courthouse.
66: 
67: If the §187 fight is lost (or §925(b) applies by statute), California law governs and §8 is void. If Meridian somehow wins the choice-of-law fight, it still needs Texas law to give it a remedy — see §4.3 — and then still needs California to recognize the judgment — it won't (`tx_jurisdiction_note.md`).
68: 
69: ### 4.3 Enforceability under Texas law (the fallback, analyzed honestly)
70: 
71: Under Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50(a) (in force), a covenant is enforceable only if **ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement** when made, and only to the extent its limits on **time, geography, and scope of activity** are reasonable and no greater than necessary to protect the promisee's business interest. §15.51(b) puts the burden on Meridian because the agreement's primary purpose is personal services. §15.52 makes these statutory criteria exclusive.
72: 
73: - **Ancillarity:** probably satisfiable. *Sheshunoff v. Johnson*, 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006), held a covenant in an at-will agreement is ancillary when the employer's return promise (e.g., providing confidential information) is performed — and it modified *Light v. Centel Cellular*, 883 S.W.3d 642 (Tex. 1994), which we cite **only for its status**: *Light*'s same-time consideration requirement is no longer law. So the fact that Zhao signed before receiving confidential information is not fatal under current Texas law. *Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011), holds stock options can supply the needed consideration link (the file references equity terms not in the excerpt — see `QUESTIONS.md`).
74: - **Reasonableness:** §8 is the problem. 24 months, nationwide, every AMR warehouse-logistics business. *Sheshunoff* enforced a one-year covenant; *Marsh* upheld a covenant tied to goodwill — neither blesses a two-year nationwide bar on an engineer's core occupation. The statute's own standard — limitations as to time, geography, and scope that are "reasonable and do not impose a greater restraint than is necessary" to protect the business interest (§15.50(a)) — is where §8 fails. (The Act file in our library covers §15.50(a), §15.51(b)–(c), §15.52 only; any further Texas limiting provisions, such as rules on restraints covering general skills, are outside the library and are not relied on here.)
75: - **The Texas answer is reformation, not invalidity:** §15.51(c) — if limitations are unreasonable, the court **shall reform** and enforce the reformed covenant, but **may not award damages for breach before reformation**. So even Meridian's best Texas-law day produces a reformed covenant (narrower time/geography/scope) and zero damages for Zhao's first months at Kestrel. Note also that the excerpt of the Act in our library covers §§15.50(a), 15.51(b)–(c), 15.52; the Texas statutory basis for injunctive relief is not in the library, so we flag rather than brief it.
76: - **And the reformed injunction dies at the state line.** Our library's Texas practice note states the conclusion directly: an injunction entered in Texas "would in any event face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds for the non-compete." Zhao lives and works in California. A Texas decree would be a paper victory Meridian pays to obtain and cannot enforce.
77: 
78: ### 4.4 Enforceability under California law
79: 
80: §16600 (as amended by SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024): "every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void," to be "read broadly, in accordance with *Edwards*... to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context... **no matter how narrowly tailored**, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter."
81: 
82: - *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP*, 44 Cal.4th 937 (2008): non-competes are void in the employment context unless a **statutory** exception applies; the Ninth Circuit's "narrow restraint" gloss was rejected, and *Campbell v. Board of Trustees*, 817 F.2d 499 (9th Cir. 1987), and *General Commercial Packaging*, 126 F.3d 1131 (9th Cir. 1997), were disapproved. We cite *Campbell* and *General Commercial Packaging* **only for their superseded status**; a narrow-restraint defense for §8 is not available. (Worth noting: even under the old narrow-restraint view, a 24-month nationwide bar on Zhao's core occupation is not "a small part of the business.")
83: - The statutory exceptions are in "this chapter"; the library contains §16600, §16600.1, and §16600.5 but **not** the sale-of-business/partnership exceptions (§§16601 et seq.), and nothing in the file suggests Zhao sold a business or partnership interest — equity compensation is not an exception the library supports. If Meridian wants an exception argument, it must come from authorities outside this library, which we cannot verify here — we note it as **unverified and unsupported on this file**, not as a defense.
84: - *Ixchel Pharma v. Biogen* (rule of reason) does not help: it applies the rule of reason to **business-to-business** restraints and expressly keeps *Edwards* governing the employment context.
85: - **No federal hook either:** the FTC Non-Compete Clause Rule, 16 C.F.R. pt. 910, was set aside nationwide in *Ryan LLC v. FTC*, 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024) — the FTC voluntarily dismissed its appeal in September 2025, and the Rule never took effect. It provides Meridian nothing, and Zhao nothing new; state law is the whole game. (We flag the Rule and *Ryan* only to close the door.)
86: 
87: Under California law, §8 is void. Our estimate of ~90–95% reflects that the only real questions are choice-of-law/venue gates, not the merits.
88: 
89: ### 4.5 Cal. Lab. Code §925 (detail in §4.1) — the forum/choice-of-law clauses are voidable
90: 
91: Summary: §925(a)–(c) + (e)–(f); no counsel, no negotiation, form contract, California residence and workplace; §15 acknowledgment contradicted by HR's own timeline. Zhao elects voidability → California forum, California law, potential §925(c) fee award. This is the most probable end of the case, and it happens before anyone briefs §15.50.
92: 
93: ### 4.6 §16600.5 exposure — Meridian's own violations
94: 
95: §16600.5 (SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024), per the library text:
96: 
97: - **(a)** Any contract void under the chapter is unenforceable "regardless of where and when the contract was signed."

41: ## 4. Analysis
42: 
43: ### 4.1 Gate one: can Meridian even keep the case in Travis County? (§925)
44: 
45: Cal. Lab. Code §925 (in force; applies to contracts entered into on or after Jan. 1, 2017 per §925(f)) bars an employer from requiring an employee "who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment," to agree to a clause that (1) requires adjudication outside California of "a claim arising in California," or (2) deprives the employee of the substantive protection of California law for a controversy arising in California. §925(a). Zhao lived and worked in Oakland for the entire employment; his claims (is §8 void? was it unlawfully enforced?) arise in California. Both §14 clauses do exactly what §925(a) prohibits.
46: 
47: The only exception, §925(e), is for an employee "in fact individually represented by legal counsel **in negotiating the terms**." The file is the opposite of that exception: standard form, "no negotiation; no attorney review requested or offered," signed 113 minutes after receipt, and §15's counsel acknowledgment is affirmatively contradicted by the HR file. Meridian drafted §15; it will not survive contact with the HR timeline, and it is itself a bad fact — a contractual recitation the company's own records dispute.
48: 
49: Consequence: §925(b) — the clauses are **voidable by the employee**, and if voided, "the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute." Zhao's resignation email already announces that he will do this. Additionally, §925(c) permits a fee award to an employee enforcing §925 rights.
50: 
51: Two honest caveats:
52: 
53: - **Whether a Texas court honors §925 is not resolved by anything in the library.** A Travis County judge does not automatically apply California statutes. Zhao's practical move is to race to California — file first for declaratory relief — which his counsel appears positioned to do. If the case ends up in a California court, §925(b) resolves the forum and choice-of-law question by statute and §187 analysis below becomes belt-and-suspenders.
54: - **Personal jurisdiction if the clause is voided.** Our library's practice note (`tx_jurisdiction_note.md`, on Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042 and *Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten*, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005)) states the forum clause generally supplies consent to jurisdiction — but if §925 voids it at Zhao's election, Texas courts would need independent minimum contacts, and "[t]wo short business trips to Austin and a contract with a Texas employer may or may not suffice." The client has now **confirmed those two trips are Zhao's entire physical Texas footprint** — exactly the fact pattern the note says "may or may not suffice." A personal-jurisdiction fight could dispose of a Travis County suit before the merits.
55: - *Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court*, 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992), is the fair counterweight: California courts respect forum/choice-of-law clauses made at arm's length. That is precisely why §925(e)'s negotiated-with-counsel carve-out exists — and why it does not fit these facts. *Ixchel Pharma v. Biogen*, 9 Cal.5th 1130 (2020), shows California enforces such clauses where the California nexus is thin (business-to-business context); Zhao's nexus — the workplace itself was California — is as thick as it gets. *Advanced Bionics Corp. v. Medtronic*, 29 Cal.4th 697 (2002), adds that in non-compete disputes California courts generally will not enjoin parallel out-of-state litigation — so Meridian should not count on a California court simply blocking a Travis County case either; interstate racing and friction are the realistic posture.
56: 
57: ### 4.2 Gate two: whose law governs enforceability? (Restatement §187; *DeSantis*; *Application Group*)
58: 
59: Both California and Texas apply Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187: the parties' chosen law applies **unless** (a) the chosen state lacks a substantial relationship, or (b) the chosen law is **contrary to a fundamental policy** of a state with a **materially greater interest** that would supply the law absent the clause. *Nedlloyd* (California); *DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.*, 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990) (Texas); `restatement_187.md`. (Texas is also in play independently: §925(b) imposes California law if Zhao voids §14; and Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.52 makes the statutory covenant rules exclusive under Texas law.)
60: 
61: Prong (a) is not Meridian's route — Texas has a substantial relationship (headquarters, R&D hub, contract administered from Austin), so the argument stands or falls on prong (b):
62: 
63: - **Fundamental policy:** California's policy voiding employment non-competes is expressly "fundamental." *Application Group, Inc. v. Hunter Group, Inc.*, 61 Cal.App.4th 881 (1998). §16600's own text (as amended by SB 699) directs broad reading.
64: - **Materially greater interest:** *Application Group* is nearly on point — a multi-state employer's non-competes with its out-of-state choice-of-law clauses did not control; California had the materially greater interest in applying §16600 to employees working for a California business. Zhao's residence, workplace, and new employment are all California. Meridian's Texas contacts are a HQ and two weeks of onsite presence.
65: - **Decisive point for venue planning:** *DeSantis* is the Texas Supreme Court doing this **against an out-of-state choice-of-law clause in a non-compete** — it refused to apply a Florida law clause for an employee working in Texas because the state with the materially greater interest had a fundamental contrary policy. The same reasoning, mirrored, tells a Travis County judge that California law supplies the rule for a California worker. Meridian cannot assume a Texas forum buys Texas law; *DeSantis* is Zhao's weapon in Meridian's chosen courthouse.
66: 
67: If the §187 fight is lost (or §925(b) applies by statute), California law governs and §8 is void. If Meridian somehow wins the choice-of-law fight, it still needs Texas law to give it a remedy — see §4.3 — and then still needs California to recognize the judgment — it won't (`tx_jurisdiction_note.md`).
68: 
69: ### 4.3 Enforceability under Texas law (the fallback, analyzed honestly)
70: 
71: Under Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50(a) (in force), a covenant is enforceable only if **ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement** when made, and only to the extent its limits on **time, geography, and scope of activity** are reasonable and no greater than necessary to protect the promisee's business interest. §15.51(b) puts the burden on Meridian because the agreement's primary purpose is personal services. §15.52 makes these statutory criteria exclusive.
72: 
73: - **Ancillarity:** probably satisfiable. *Sheshunoff v. Johnson*, 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006), held a covenant in an at-will agreement is ancillary when the employer's return promise (e.g., providing confidential information) is performed — and it modified *Light v. Centel Cellular*, 883 S.W.3d 642 (Tex. 1994), which we cite **only for its status**: *Light*'s same-time consideration requirement is no longer law. So the fact that Zhao signed before receiving confidential information is not fatal under current Texas law. *Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011), holds stock options can supply the needed consideration link (the file references equity terms not in the excerpt — see `QUESTIONS.md`).
74: - **Reasonableness:** §8 is the problem. 24 months, nationwide, every AMR warehouse-logistics business. *Sheshunoff* enforced a one-year covenant; *Marsh* upheld a covenant tied to goodwill — neither blesses a two-year nationwide bar on an engineer's core occupation. The statute's own standard — limitations as to time, geography, and scope that are "reasonable and do not impose a greater restraint than is necessary" to protect the business interest (§15.50(a)) — is where §8 fails. (The Act file in our library covers §15.50(a), §15.51(b)–(c), §15.52 only; any further Texas limiting provisions, such as rules on restraints covering general skills, are outside the library and are not relied on here.)
75: - **The Texas answer is reformation, not invalidity:** §15.51(c) — if limitations are unreasonable, the court **shall reform** and enforce the reformed covenant, but **may not award damages for breach before reformation**. So even Meridian's best Texas-law day produces a reformed covenant (narrower time/geography/scope) and zero damages for Zhao's first months at Kestrel. Note also that the excerpt of the Act in our library covers §§15.50(a), 15.51(b)–(c), 15.52; the Texas statutory basis for injunctive relief is not in the library, so we flag rather than brief it.
76: - **And the reformed injunction dies at the state line.** Our library's Texas practice note states the conclusion directly: an injunction entered in Texas "would in any event face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds for the non-compete." Zhao lives and works in California. A Texas decree would be a paper victory Meridian pays to obtain and cannot enforce.
77: 
78: ### 4.4 Enforceability under California law
79: 
80: §16600 (as amended by SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024): "every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void," to be "read broadly, in accordance with *Edwards*... to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context... **no matter how narrowly tailored**, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter."
81: 
82: - *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP*, 44 Cal.4th 937 (2008): non-competes are void in the employment context unless a **statutory** exception applies; the Ninth Circuit's "narrow restraint" gloss was rejected, and *Campbell v. Board of Trustees*, 817 F.2d 499 (9th Cir. 1987), and *General Commercial Packaging*, 126 F.3d 1131 (9th Cir. 1997), were disapproved. We cite *Campbell* and *General Commercial Packaging* **only for their superseded status**; a narrow-restraint defense for §8 is not available. (Worth noting: even under the old narrow-restraint view, a 24-month nationwide bar on Zhao's core occupation is not "a small part of the business.")
83: - The statutory exceptions are in "this chapter"; the library contains §16600, §16600.1, and §16600.5 but **not** the sale-of-business/partnership exceptions (§§16601 et seq.), and nothing in the file suggests Zhao sold a business or partnership interest — equity compensation is not an exception the library supports. If Meridian wants an exception argument, it must come from authorities outside this library, which we cannot verify here — we note it as **unverified and unsupported on this file**, not as a defense.
84: - *Ixchel Pharma v. Biogen* (rule of reason) does not help: it applies the rule of reason to **business-to-business** restraints and expressly keeps *Edwards* governing the employment context.
85: - **No federal hook either:** the FTC Non-Compete Clause Rule, 16 C.F.R. pt. 910, was set aside nationwide in *Ryan LLC v. FTC*, 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024) — the FTC voluntarily dismissed its appeal in September 2025, and the Rule never took effect. It provides Meridian nothing, and Zhao nothing new; state law is the whole game. (We flag the Rule and *Ryan* only to close the door.)
86: 
87: Under California law, §8 is void. Our estimate of ~90–95% reflects that the only real questions are choice-of-law/venue gates, not the merits.
88: 
89: ### 4.5 Cal. Lab. Code §925 (detail in §4.1) — the forum/choice-of-law clauses are voidable
90: 
91: Summary: §925(a)–(c) + (e)–(f); no counsel, no negotiation, form contract, California residence and workplace; §15 acknowledgment contradicted by HR's own timeline. Zhao elects voidability → California forum, California law, potential §925(c) fee award. This is the most probable end of the case, and it happens before anyone briefs §15.50.
92: 
93: ### 4.6 §16600.5 exposure — Meridian's own violations
94: 
95: §16600.5 (SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024), per the library text:
96: 
97: - **(a)** Any contract void under the chapter is unenforceable "regardless of where and when the contract was signed."
98: - **(b)** An employer "shall not **attempt to enforce**" a void contract "regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California."

100: - **(d)** An employer that **enters into** such a contract **or attempts to enforce** one "commits a civil violation."
101: - **(e)** The employee may sue for **injunctive relief or actual damages**; a **prevailing employee shall recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs**.

190: 4. Whether the §8 form has gone to other California hires since Jan. 1, 2024 (each a potential §16600.5(c) violation).
191: 5. The *Alvarez* outcome and full texts of *Calderon* / *Westbrook* en banc (prior firm advice unverifiable; not relied upon).
192: 
193: ## 10. Addendum — GC Questions (Dana, Oct. 25, 2026): *Calderon*/*Westbrook* and the FTC Rule
194: 
195: **Q1: "Our outside counsel's 2024 memo says *Calderon* and *Westbrook* support exactly this. Why aren't you relying on them?"**
196: 
197: Three reasons; each is independently sufficient not to rely on them.
198: 
199: 1. **They are unverifiable.** Both cases appear *only inside the firm's own memos* (`memo_bank/`); they are not in the library, and no full text exists anywhere in this file (the client confirmed no additional information). An engagement standard this office has applied to every authority — verify status or label unverified — applies equally to the firm's own prior advice. Cases we cannot read cannot be load-bearing for a filing decision.
200: 2. **The firm itself flagged them as unsettled.** The 2025 update records that the Ninth Circuit **granted rehearing en banc in *Westbrook*** (argued Jan. 2025) and describes the position as maintained "pending further guidance." As of today there is no record of the en banc outcome. Betting a Travis County filing — and the §16600.5(b) exposure that filing creates — on an appellate status nobody in the file can confirm is not advice; it is a wager.
201: 3. **Even taken exactly as the 2024 memo characterizes them, they do not fit these facts:**
202:    - *Westbrook* is described as holding "§16600.5 does not apply extraterritorially to contracts with out-of-state employers" — a theory whose premise is employment maintained **outside** California. The client has confirmed Zhao's employment was maintained **entirely in California** (Oakland the whole time; Austin = two trips). Whatever *Westbrook* holds, this is not its case. And the library's statutory text points the other way: §16600.5(b) reaches attempts to enforce "**regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California**."
203:    - *Calderon* is described as enforcing a Texas choice-of-law clause against a remote California employee who "availed himself" of Texas benefits. Zhao's entire Texas "benefit" record is two short trips and a form contract signed in 113 minutes with no counsel and no negotiation. More fundamentally, **§925 is a statute** that makes exactly such clauses voidable for employees who primarily reside and work in California, with a carve-out only for employees "in fact individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating the terms" — the file shows none. As characterized, *Calderon* never engages §925 at all; a case we cannot read does not override a statute we can.
204:    - Neither case — as characterized — addresses the other two gates at all: §925's forum-voidability and the §187/*DeSantis* analysis. *DeSantis* is **Texas Supreme Court precedent binding in Travis County**, and it does precisely what Dana wants undone: it refuses to apply a contrary out-of-state law clause in a non-compete for the state with the materially greater interest and a fundamental contrary policy. Even a true believer in the 2024 memo's two cases must still win every gate.
205: 
206: **Q2: "The FTC rule is dead, so what's the problem?"**
207: 
208: The FTC Non-Compete Clause Rule would have **banned** non-competes — it was a sword against employers like Meridian, never a shield. Its set-aside (*Ryan LLC v. FTC*, N.D. Tex. 2024; appeal dismissed Sept. 2025, per the library) takes nothing away from Meridian because **Zhao's case never needed it**. Zhao's case rests on California statutes that long predate the FTC rule and are untouched by its death: §16600 (employment non-competes void, "no matter how narrowly tailored"), §16600.1 (unlawful to include; notice duty; UCL treatment), §16600.5 (no attempting to enforce; private action; prevailing employee recovers fees), and Lab. Code §925 (voidable forum/choice-of-law clauses). The firm's own 2025 update concedes the frame: "With the FTC rule enjoined, **state law controls**." The state law that controls here is California's — and that is the whole problem, FTC rule or no FTC rule.

The statute's own standard — limitations as to time, geography, and scope that are "reasonable and do not impose a greater restraint than is necessary" to protect the business interest (§15.50(a)) — is where §8 fails.  §16600 (as amended by SB 699, eff. -- *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP*, 44 Cal.4th 937 (2008): non-competes are void in the employment context unless a **statutory** exception applies; the Ninth Circuit's "narrow restraint" gloss was rejected, and *Campbell v. Board of Trustees*, 817 F.2d 499 (9th Cir. 1987), and *General Commercial Packaging*, 126 F.3d 1131 (9th Cir. 1997), were disapproved. We cite *Campbell* and *General Commercial Packaging* **only for their superseded status**; a narrow-restraint defense for §8 is not available. 111: §16600.1 (AB 1076, eff. Jan. 1, 2024): (a) it is **unlawful to include** a non-compete in an employment contract (or to require an employee to enter one) that does not satisfy a statutory exception; (b) for **current employees**, and **former employees employed after Jan. 1, 2022**, whose contracts include such a clause, the employer **shall notify the employee by Feb. 14, 2024**, in a written individualized communication delivered to last known address **and** email, that the clause is void; (c) a violation "constitutes an act of unfair competition within the meaning of Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200)."
112: 
113: Two findings for Meridian:
114: 
115: - **As to Zhao:** §16600.1(a) was violated when §8 went into his March 4, 2024 contract — 63 days after (a) took effect. The (b) *notice* duty is genuinely ambiguous for him: the deadline (Feb. 14, 2024) came **14 days before Meridian even made the offer** and 19 days before he was hired. One reading says a hire after the deadline never triggers the fixed-date duty; the other says he became a "current employee" whose contract contained a void clause and notice was owed within a reasonable time. The library contains only the statutory text; no case resolving this is in the library, so we flag it as **unverified on the case law**. Either way, the absence of notice changes nothing about §8's voidness — but see the next point.
116: - **As to everyone else — the bigger problem:** Legal ops ticket LO-233 records that the AB 1076 notice project was "deprioritized" and **no notice was sent to California employees, company-wide**. For every current California employee and post-2022 former California employee with a §8-style clause, the plain text of (b) was violated by the Feb. 14, 2024 deadline, and each violation is a UCL act under (c). This exposure is independent of Zhao and probably larger than Zhao. The number of affected people is **unknown — the client has no additional information** (§9, `QUESTIONS.md`). (The UCL remedies themselves are outside the library — §§17200 et seq. are not in it — so we flag rather than quantify them.)
117: - **The LO-233 entry is the worst document in the file** on the knowledge question, and it has gotten worse. As of February 2024, Legal had an AB 1076 notice project on the books; the record shows the project "deprioritized," **no** notice sent to California employees, and the ticket ultimately closed as **"won't do"** (client-confirmed Oct. 25, 2026). That is a documented, deliberate decision not to comply — not an oversight — and on March 4, 2024, after the February 14 statutory deadline had passed, Meridian put a new void non-compete into a new California hire's contract. If Zhao ever litigates willfulness-adjacent theories, that is the exhibit. The affected population (current employees plus former employees after Jan. 1, 2022, with §8-style clauses working in California) is **unknown — the client has no additional information** — so we cannot quantify this exposure and we do not force it to a number.
118: 
119: ### 4.8 Remedies and fee exposure (illustrative arithmetic)
120: 
121: The excerpt contains **no fee-shifting clause and no liquidated-damages clause**; the complete agreement was not provided and the client reports no additional documents, so we assume none and flag this as an unresolved unknown. The exposure grid below uses **assumed rates** — no rate card is in the file — and shows the arithmetic so it can be corrected.
122: 
123: | Scenario | Meridian's own fees (assumed) | Fee exposure to Zhao | Notes |
124: |---|---|---|---|
125: | A. Sue in Travis County | 250–500 h × $400/h = **$100k–$200k** | §925(c) + §16600.5(e)(2): if Zhao prevails, his fees shift: 150–400 h × $450–$600/h = **$67.5k–$240k** | Win rate ~5–10% (§2). PJ + §925 motion likely disposes of case early: 250 h × $400 = $100k typical exit cost. |
126: | B. Demand letter invoking §8 | $10k–$30k | Completes §16600.5(b) violation → Zhao's injunction + fees claim, ~70–85% fee award | 150 h × $500 = **$75k** to Zhao plus our letter cost. Actively harmful. |
127: | C. Do nothing | $0 | Residual: Zhao sues for declaration/§16600.5 anyway (~25–45%) | His damages claim is thin if Meridian never enforces, but the (c)-signing violation already exists, and the confirmed "won't do" record plus zero misappropriation evidence make his suit cleaner and his counsel's fee model more attractive — hence the small increase from our pre-confirmation estimate of ~20–40%. |
128: | D. Send §16600.1(b)-style notice that §8 is void | ~$0–$15k | Removes the "live dispute" predicate for Zhao's remaining claims; his only retained theory (the 2024 signing violation) loses its damages and much of its fee attraction | Also cures, prospectively, the company-wide AB 1076 notice failure. |
129: 
130: Even in the worst plausible case, Scenario A costs Meridian roughly **$170k–$440k** (own fees + shifted fees, arithmetic shown above) to buy a 5–10% chance at an injunction that the library's Texas practice note says California will not recognize anyway. Zhao's own actual damages are currently small (he started at Kestrel on schedule; no lost income shown), so the money at stake is **fees**, on both sides.
131: 
132: ## 5. Strongest Argument for Each Side
133: 
134: **Meridian's best:** The choice-of-law/forum clauses are presumptively valid — Texas has a substantial relationship (HQ, R&D hub, Austin-administered hiring), and under *Nedlloyd* arm's-length clauses command deference; §15 recites Zhao had the opportunity to consult counsel. If a Texas court applies Texas law, §15.50(a)/§15.51(c) guarantees *some* enforceable covenant — *Sheshunoff* and *Marsh* establish that confidential-information promises and equity support ancillary covenants — and Meridian at least gets reformation rather than total invalidity. **Candidly: this argument's load-bearing pieces are the §15 recital (contradicted by the HR file) and the assumption that Texas law applies (contradicted by *DeSantis*). It is the weakest form of the case, and it still ends at the California border.**
135: 
136: **Zhao's best:** §925. The statute does the work on the employer's own documents: California residence and workplace, form contract, 113-minute signing, no counsel, no negotiation, and a contractual recital the company's HR timeline refutes. Once §14 is voidable and voided, §925(b) supplies the California forum and California law by statute; §16600 then voids §8 without any balancing; and §16600.5(c)–(d) means Meridian was already in violation the day it hired him. He has added, by his resignation email, that he has California counsel who has told him exactly this. And the client's own confirmation — no evidence he took anything; "the competing itself" is the objection — concedes the case is about a pure restraint of trade, which is precisely what §16600 voids.
137: 
138: ## 6. Recommendation
139: 
140: 1. **Do not file in Travis County.** Do not issue any demand letter, notice, or communication that invokes §8 to restrain Zhao's Kestrel employment. (This also means: no "preservation" letters to Kestrel that demand Zhao stop working — they are attempts to enforce.)
141: 2. **Send a §16600.1(b)-conforming notice to Zhao** — individualized written notice, by mail to last known address and email, stating §8 is void and Meridian will not seek to enforce it. Have counsel send it, not the line manager.
142: 3. **Inventory the company-wide AB 1076 failure now.** Identify all current employees and former employees (employed after Jan. 1, 2022) with §8-style clauses who primarily work in California, and send conforming notices. The affected population is currently unknown to the client — the inventory itself is step one. LO-233 was closed "won't do" in or around February 2024; the UCL exposure under §16600.1(c) compounds with every employee left un-noticed. This is a bigger liability than Zhao and it is fixable.
143: 4. **Fix the form.** The same §8 went into a California hire's contract 19 days after the AB 1076 notice deadline passed. Every new California-based hire signing this form is a fresh §16600.5(c) violation. Remove §8 for California-based hires (and check whether Meridian has used the form elsewhere; that is beyond this library's scope).
144: 5. **Do not build a §10 case that does not exist.** The client confirms there is no evidence Zhao accessed, took, or retained anything, and that the objection is to the competing itself — which §8 cannot lawfully reach and §10 does not either. Zhao affirmatively states he will honor confidentiality. §10 (confidentiality/inventions) and §9 (12-month non-solicit) are separate covenants whose California-law treatment is not briefed in this library; on this record there is no trade-secret case to bring, and §8 must not be enforced as a proxy for §10. If actual misuse evidence ever emerges, that is a different case requiring authorities beyond this file.
145: 6. **Reconsider reliance on the 2024/2025 firm memos** (the memo-bank files in the library). Their core support — *Calderon* and *Westbrook* — is unverifiable on this library, and the 2025 update itself notes rehearing en banc was granted in *Westbrook*. The 2024 memo's recommendation to sue in Travis County in the *Alvarez* matter rests on the same sand and should not drive this decision.
146: 7. **Watch for Zhao's declaratory/§16600.5 action.** If filed, the realistic settlement posture is: notice letter confirming §8 void + §10 reaffirmation, early, before fees accrue.
147: 8. **On the request not to memorialize the "won't do" decision: the exposure is managed by curing it, not by quiet.** Candidly, and because you asked for straight advice: we cannot leave that fact out of our analysis — it is load-bearing for the company-wide exposure opinion, and it is already in writing in your own records (ticket LO-233) and now in your communication with us. No advice we can give removes a completed statutory violation; only the §16600.1(b) notices do that prospectively, per employee, as sent. Legitimate hygiene is available and we recommend all of it: this memo and our exchanges are privileged legal advice; further factual development and any remediation plan should run through counsel; and the company should not create *new* records restating a decision not to comply, because each such decision is itself the violation. What we will not do is paper over the existing record or advise suppressing it — and nothing in this file needs to be disclosed to Zhao or anyone else beyond the voidness notices themselves.

149: ## 7. Authorities Verification Table
150:

Pacific Dynamics Corp.*, 48 Cal.App.5th 1120 (2023); *Westbrook Systems, Inc. v. Ng*, 91 F.4th 1033 (9th Cir. 2024)) are **not** in the library, were not verified, and are not cited as authority.

179: 
180: All date arithmetic in §3 is reproducible: 113 min signing; 63 days between statutes' effective date and signing; AB 1076 deadline 14 days before the offer email, 19 days before hire; 940-day employment; 13-day gap to Kestrel; 731-day restraint window; 706 days remaining as of Oct. 25, 2026. Fee figures in §4.8 are illustrative on assumed hours/rates — no rate data exists in the file. These are labeled as assumptions; nothing has been forced to balance.

182: ## 9. Open Items (updated after client responses of Oct. 25, 2026)
183: 
184: Closed by client responses: Zhao's Texas footprint (two trips only; all other work Oakland — §925 facts confirmed, *Michiana* fallback narrowed); whether Zhao took anything (no evidence; objection is the competing itself — no §10/trade-secret case on this record); LO-233 status (never sent; closed "won't do" — exposure treated as a documented non-compliance).
185: 
186: Still open, and the client has **no additional information** on them — flagged explicitly, not resolved:
187: 1. Whether signing was a condition of employment (drives §925(a)); analyzed as a well-supported assumption.
188: 2. The full executed agreement (any fee-shifting? severability? equity terms bearing on the *Marsh* argument?). Assumed none.
189: 3. The company-wide AB 1076 population (current + post-2022 former California employees with §8-style clauses). Unquantified; inventory recommended.

191: 5. The *Alvarez* outcome and full texts of *Calderon* / *Westbrook* en banc (prior firm advice unverifiable; not relied upon).

193: ## 10. Addendum — GC Questions (Dana, Oct. 25, 2026): *Calderon*/*Westbrook* and the FTC Rule
194: 
195: **Q1: "Our outside counsel's 2024 memo says *Calderon* and *Westbrook* support exactly this. Why aren't you relying on them?"**
196: 
197: Three reasons; each is independently sufficient not to rely on them.
198: 
199: 1. **They are unverifiable.** Both cases appear *only inside the firm's own memos* (`memo_bank/`); they are not in the library, and no full text exists anywhere in this file (the client confirmed no additional information). An engagement standard this office has applied to every authority — verify status or label unverified — applies equally to the firm's own prior advice. Cases we cannot read cannot be load-bearing for a filing decision.
200: 2. **The firm itself flagged them as unsettled.** The 2025 update records that the Ninth Circuit **granted rehearing en banc in *Westbrook*** (argued Jan. 2025) and describes the position as maintained "pending further guidance." As of today there is no record of the en banc outcome. Betting a Travis County filing — and the §16600.5(b) exposure that filing creates — on an appellate status nobody in the file can confirm is not advice; it is a wager.
201: 3. **Even taken exactly as the 2024 memo characterizes them, they do not fit these facts:**
202:    - *Westbrook* is described as holding "§16600.5 does not apply extraterritorially to contracts with out-of-state employers" — a theory whose premise is employment maintained **outside** California. The client has confirmed Zhao's employment was maintained **entirely in California** (Oakland the whole time; Austin = two trips). Whatever *Westbrook* holds, this is not its case. And the library's statutory text points the other way: §16600.5(b) reaches attempts to enforce "**regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California**."
203:    - *Calderon* is described as enforcing a Texas choice-of-law clause against a remote California employee who "availed himself" of Texas benefits. Zhao's entire Texas "benefit" record is two short trips and a form contract signed in 113 minutes with no counsel and no negotiation. More fundamentally, **§925 is a statute** that makes exactly such clauses voidable for employees who primarily reside and work in California, with a carve-out only for employees "in fact individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating the terms" — the file shows none. As characterized, *Calderon* never engages §925 at all; a case we cannot read does not override a statute we can.
204:    - Neither case — as characterized — addresses the other two gates at all: §925's forum-voidability and the §187/*DeSantis* analysis. *DeSantis* is **Texas Supreme Court precedent binding in Travis County**, and it does precisely what Dana wants undone: it refuses to apply a contrary out-of-state law clause in a non-compete for the state with the materially greater interest and a fundamental contrary policy. Even a true believer in the 2024 memo's two cases must still win every gate.
